papers.title: Projected intensification of soil salinization in global drylands under future aridity increase
papers.abstract: Abstract Soil salinization threatens agricultural production, water management, and ecosystem health. Yet, how increasing aridity will reshape 21st-century soil salinity patterns across drylands, particularly in croplands, remains unclear. Here, we compile a relatively comprehensive global soil salinity dataset from the past two decades, projecting future dryland soil salinity dynamics using climate-driven machine learning models with multiple covariates, including dynamic dryland extent and human influences. Our results show an 8% expansion of global drylands saline soils under increasing aridity by 2100 (SSP5-8.5) relative to 2004–2023. Southwestern US, Mexico, southern Europe, central South America, eastern and southern Africa are highest-risk hotspots. We further show dryland croplands face serious salinization, especially irrigated systems, where half of these newly salinized areas project more than 4.9% (maize), 17.2% (dryland rice), 3.3% (sorghum), and 21.2% (wheat) potential production losses. Our findings inform long-term adaptation strategies to mitigate emerging salinization risks and sustain water and food security.

papers.title: Brassinosteroids improve nitrogen utilization by antagonizing BIN2-mediated SnRK1 activation
A HAT7/ATHB13/Brassinosteroid signaling module mediates growth of laticifer cells in Euphorbia lathyris
papers.abstract: Abstract Laticifers, the coenocytic cells responsible for latex production, represent one of the most extreme examples of continuous and polarized growth in plants. Their unique architecture, extending over large distances, requires tight coordination between wall extensibility, cytoplasmic organization, and hormonal control. Here, we characterized the poor in latex 13 (pil13) mutant of Euphorbia lathyris which, similar to the previously described pil1 and pil6 mutants, is defective in laticifer expansion during post-embryonic phases of plant growth. Through comparative transcriptomic analyses of these three pil mutants, we identified a core set of 266 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) that define a transcriptomic signature associated with laticifers. We further identified a regulatory network linking two HD-Zip I transcription factors, HAT7 and ATHB13, with brassinosteroid (BR) signaling in the mediation of laticifer growth. This HAT7/ATHB13–BR module regulates the expression of laticifer DEGs involved in cell wall remodeling. Consequently, we found that laticifer cell walls are highly enriched in low-esterified homogalacturonan (HG) and branched rhamnogalacturonan-I (RG-I) pectins. Whole-mount immunolocalization revealed that laticifer cell walls exhibit a peculiar spatial segregation of pectic polysaccharides. These pectins follow a characteristic complementary, non-overlapping deposition pattern along the laticifer longitudinal axis, presumably conferring both elasticity and mechanical integrity. This modular pectin assembly appears compatible with the high flexibility and mechanical sinuosity required for growing of laticifers through host tissues, while accommodating internal turgor pressure changes derived from latex accumulation. Our findings define the laticifer as a cellular model in which wall remodeling, cell growth, turgor pressure, and hormonal signaling are mechanistically coupled.

papers.title: A CRC–MYB chromatin loop controls auxin-mediated nectary growth in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Abstract Floral nectaries, typically located at stamen bases, secrete sugar-rich nectar containing diverse secondary metabolites. Despite their defined position and specialized function, the mechanisms governing nectary formation remain unclear. Using publicly available single-nucleus RNA-seq data and newly generated spatial transcriptomic data, we identify a putative ordering of transcriptional states associated with nectary development and a spatial regulatory network controlling nectary growth in Arabidopsis thaliana . We further show that CRABS CLAW (CRC) is central to this network, integrating transcriptional regulation with spatial auxin transport and pathways controlling phytohormone signaling, sugar transport and terpene biosynthesis. CRC interacts with MYB21, MYB24 and MYB57 to form a complex that binds the 5′ and 3′ regulatory regions of MACCHI-BOU 4 ( MAB4 ), promoting a chromatin loop that enhances MAB4 expression and supports proper nectary size. MAB4 reinforces PIN-FORMED 1-mediated auxin transport to establish auxin maxima at the nectary tip and regulates PIN6 localization to maintain auxin gradients. These findings link transcriptional regulation and auxin transport with nectary organogenesis and metabolic function.

papers.title: Sustainable solar water purification: Exploring the structural advantages of higher plants
papers.abstract: Solar vapor generation is a promising technique for water purification, although the development of efficient and sustainable systems for practical use remains challenging. Here, we introduce a higher plant–derived evaporator, leveraging the structural advantages of plants and the synergistic integration of multiple components, including carbon black–coated ultrathin wood slices with perforated pores, nanocellulose aerogel, and vertically aligned wheat straws. This configuration facilitates low-tortuosity water transport within the internal framework while promoting interfacial evaporation at its surface. Under 1 sun, the evaporator achieved an evaporation rate of up to 3.2 kilograms per square meter (kg m −2 ) per hour. The material’s scalability and the capability to continuously collect clean water in outdoor environments were successfully demonstrated. Outdoors, under a solar intensity of 0.5 to 0.9 sun, the assembled device achieved a daily fresh water yield of up to 10.9 kg m −2 from seawater. With highly accessible renewable raw materials, low production cost, and exceptional water purification efficiency, this cost-effective solar evaporator is edge closer to viable, real-world applications.

papers.title: Loss of tRNA uridine thiolation affects mRNA translation, protein production, and metabolite accumulation in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: It is well established in yeast and animal system that the level of uridine thiolation at position 34 of tRNA anticodon loops can impact the decoding potential of the corresponding codons. Using Arabidopsis thaliana , we confirm that the ability of the plant ribosome to decode AAA, GAA, and CAA codons is impaired when this thiol group is lost, leading to a reduction in protein production, especially for genes enriched in these codons. Interestingly, we observed that loss of tRNA thiolation results in variations in the levels of numerous proteins involved in sulfur-compound metabolism and amino acid biosynthesis. These variations, in turn, affect the accumulation of several sulfur-containing metabolites and amino acids, suggesting that the level of tRNA thiolation has a direct and profound impact on plant metabolism. We also demonstrate that U 34 thiolation is essential for adjusting plant growth in response to sulfur limitation and that its absence directly affects the plant’s interaction with bacteria, including both pathogens and beneficial organisms. Our results support the hypothesis that the level of tRNA thiolation can be used in plant to link nutritional status to translation.

papers.title: A transposon inserted into HELD1 repressed maize husk leaf blade extension during maize domestication
papers.abstract: Husk leaves are the closest photosynthetic organs to the ear, which contribute directly to grain filling and have potential for yield improvement in maize. Teosinte has a long husk extended leaf blade, whereas maize exhibits a reduced or even no husk leaf blade. However, the genetic basis of this transition in the husk leaf during domestication remains unknown. In this study, we identified a major quantitative trait locus (QTL), Husk Extended Leaf Blade 1 ( HELD1 ), corresponding to the tassels replace upper ears1 ( tru1 ) gene. A 133-base pair (bp) Harbinger transposon inserted into the tru1 intron introduces two TEOSINTE BRANCHED 1 (TB1) binding motifs, thereby recruiting TB1 to directly enhance tru1 transcription. Further analyses revealed that TRU1 interacts with the transcription factor ALOG1, which in turn enhances the expression of liguleless2 ( lg2 ), a key regulator of ligule development. Together with brassinosteroid-deficient dwarf1 ( brd1 ) and GA2ox1 , these genes set up a regulatory network that defines the ligular-auricular position, controls the leaf blade-to-husk (sheath) ratio in husk and stem leaves, and regulates husk leaf blade length. Population genetic analyses indicate that HELD1 experienced significant human selection, resulting in the transposon insertion becoming the dominant allele in domesticated maize. Additionally, the teosinte HELD1 allele with extended husk leaf blades significantly enhances yield in maize. Our results demonstrate HELD1 is an important regulator of husk and stem leaf architectures, contributing to the ligular-auricular position to adjust the ratio of leaf blade to husk or sheath.

papers.title: Transcriptional control of meiotic recombination by DREAM complex components
papers.abstract: Meiotic chromosome segregation and recombination, essential for sexual reproduction and evolution, require a specialized gene set. Despite its importance, the transcriptional regulators that directly orchestrate meiotic gene expression remain unidentified in plants. We identify the MuvB core components known from the DREAM complex as key transcriptional regulators of meiotic recombination in Arabidopsis . Loss of DREAM components TCX5/6 and ALY1/2 leads to impaired recombination and fertility defects. Meiocyte-specific transcriptome profiling and genome-wide binding analyses reveal that core recombination genes, including the crossover-promoting helicase MER3, are direct targets. Consistently, MER3 overexpression partially rescues recombination defects in DREAM-compromised plants. These findings establish the DREAM complex components as important regulators of the meiotic program in plants. Given that DREAM dysfunction causes reproductive defects in animals, this regulatory role may be conserved across multicellular eukaryotes.

papers.title: Publisher Correction: Gb3 encodes a unique kinase fusion protein conferring greenbug resistance in wheat
Regulation of target gene expression by chromatin-associated protein-coding transcripts in plants
papers.abstract: Protein-coding transcripts are regarded as intermediates that mediate DNA-to-protein information flow, leaving their noncoding regulatory potential largely underappreciated. Genome-wide profiling of RNA–chromatin interactions in Arabidopsis has uncovered widespread associations between protein-coding transcripts and distinct genomic loci, implying that they possess regulatory functions. Here, we found that BT2 and GSL8 transcripts modulate target gene transcription independently of their protein products through distinct mechanisms. The BT2 transcript represses transcription of its targets CEP2 and MRF4 by forming RNA–DNA triplexes, thereby restricting root growth and promoting flowering, whereas GSL8 acts through a triplex-independent pathway. Our findings unveil intrinsic regulatory activities of protein-coding transcripts, challenging the canonical definition of mRNA function and blurring the functional distinction between coding and noncoding RNAs in the context of genome evolution.

papers.title: Glycan recognition by a plant damage-sensing immune receptor
papers.abstract: Pathogens target and degrade the extracellular matrix surrounding plant cells. A central question is how cell wall–derived damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) are recognized and integrated to trigger immune responses. We address this question by determining the structure of the extracellular multidomain of the impaired in glycan perception 1 (IGP1) receptor in both apo form and bound to the cellulose-derived DAMP cellotriose. Structural analyses reveal that constitutive interactions of leucine-rich repeat (LRR)–malectin domains preconfigure IGP1 for ligand recognition and that the receptor features a highly specific sugar-binding pocket in the LRR domain capable of distinguishing fine variations in glycan structures. By directly sensing cello-oligomers, IGP1 operates as a cell wall surveillance receptor that links pathogen-induced wall degradation to immune alerting, equipping plants to mount rapid and robust defense responses.

papers.title: Abiotic conversion of nitrate to ammonium enhances nitrogen use efficiency in paddy soils
papers.abstract: Nitrogen (N) use efficiency is critical in ensuring food production while reducing nitrate (NO 3 − -N) to ammonium (NH 4 + -N) is widely recognized as a key for reducing N loss from paddy fields. Microbial involvement has long been regarded as the indispensable step for NO 3 − -N reduction to NH 4 + -N in nature; it remains largely unknown whether abiotic processes can drive this. Here, using laser confocal fluorescence microscopy and thermodynamic laws, we find that Fe(II) ions in the rice rhizosphere exist on iron plaque in a specific manner with strong reducing capability. These specifically adsorbed Fe(II) ions (Fe(II) SA ) could mediate the abiotic reduction of NO 3 − -N to NH 4 + -N, accounting for 57% of the total NO 3 − -N reduction. When cultured in a sterile nutrient solution containing only 15 NO 3 − -N and Fe(II) ions, over 90% of N in the xylem of rice plants exists as 15 NH 4 + -N, directly proving the occurrence of NO 3 − -N reduction to NH 4 + -N and taken up by rice. Theoretical calculations elucidate the Fe(II) SA -induced local electron depolarization enhances interfacial charge transfer which drives this reaction with the conversion of *NO to *NOH/*NHO identified as the rate-limiting step. We then propose a regulatory strategy to establish a stable Fe(II) SA /Fe(III) SA cycle utilizing FeC for controlled-release of Fe(II) ions. Two-year field experiments confirmed this strategy can increase rice yield by 16.1% while cutting half of the N input. Our work enables the design of novel pathways in improving N use efficiency for sustainable rice production.
papers.affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Regional environment and Sustainability, Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences

papers.title: From stress perception to metabolite disposition: dynamic regulation of stilbene biosynthesis in plants
papers.abstract: Abstract Stilbenes are inducible plant specialized metabolites, best exemplified by resveratrol, a phytoalexin that links environmental perception, defense responses, and phenylpropanoid resource allocation. Stilbene accumulation may be controlled at three mechanistically distinct levels: signaling cascades that connect environmental and hormonal cues to kinase-dependent activation; combinatorial transcriptional control, which governs the response amplitude and specificity of stilbene synthase (STS) genes; and branch selection together with product disposition, which shapes the final metabolic output. Within this framework, MYB and WRKY proteins serve as major transcriptional nodes as activators or repressors, yet their regulatory effects depend on combinatorial interactions, phosphorylation events, competitive promoter occupancy, and metabolic context. We explicitly distinguish strongly supported mechanisms, defined by genetic perturbation, direct target validation, and metabolite quantification from emerging models built primarily on transient expression assays or co-expression correlations. This distinction avoids equating regulators supported by disparate levels of experimental evidence, identifies the most robust principles governing pathway control, and highlights experiments required to turn descriptive associations into causal mechanistic models. We further highlight conceptual insights extending beyond stilbene metabolism to inducible specialized metabolism in general, and outline research priorities for comparative genetics, cell-resolved analysis, and predictive pathway engineering.

papers.title: Structure-based targeting of Atg8 uncovers its essential role in autophagy-mediated detoxification
papers.abstract: Autophagy degrades and recycles intracellular material, allowing cells to maintain homeostasis and adapt to environmental stress. In the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae , the core autophagy protein MoAtg8 is required for autophagosome formation and host infection. Here, we determined the crystal structure of MoAtg8 and used it for structure-guided virtual screening of a focused compound library enriched for natural products and autophagy-related molecules. This screen identified nordihydroguaiaretic acid (NDGA), a naturally occurring lignan, as a MoAtg8-binding compound. NDGA suppressed conidial germination and appressorium formation, disrupted membrane integrity, and reduced pathogenicity in M. oryzae , with no detectable phytotoxicity to rice under the conditions tested. Mechanistically, the 5-lipoxygenase Mo5Lox, a target of NDGA, bound NDGA with lower affinity than MoAtg8. MoAtg8 associated with NDGA through Gln81 and promoted its autophagy-dependent delivery to vacuoles, thereby reducing compound availability to toxicity-associated targets. Disruption of autophagy or mutation of Gln81 in MoAtg8 increased fungal sensitivity to NDGA. These findings identify an autophagy-mediated detoxification route for an exogenous antifungal compound and reveal how MoAtg8-dependent trafficking modulates NDGA efficacy in a plant-pathogenic fungus.
papers.affiliation: State Key Laboratory for Quality and Safety of Agro-products, Zhejiang Provincial Key Laboratory of Agricultural Microbiomics, Institute of Biotechnology, Zhejiang University

papers.title: Structural basis for size-selective perception of chitin in plants
papers.abstract: Plants detect microbes through pattern recognition receptors that perceive conserved microbial surface motifs known as microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs). Lysin motif (LysM) receptors recognize and mediate downstream responses to chitinous MAMPs. In this study, we elucidated the mechanism for the specific recognition of long-chain chitin oligomers and identified a hallmark bridge domain characteristic of the CHITIN PERCEPTION (CHIP) receptor class. Structural analysis of receptor-ligand complexes, biochemistry, and in planta functional studies of inhibitory nanobodies revealed the mechanism of size-selective, high-affinity chitin perception in Lotus japonicus and Medicago truncatula . Additionally, we identified the CHITIN ELICITOR RECEPTOR KINASE (CERK) class as low-affinity, yet essential, co-receptors and propose a mechanistic model for a ligand-induced core signaling heterocomplex. Our findings establish the structural and mechanistic basis of differential chitin perception and receptor complex assembly in chitin-elicited plant immune signaling.
papers.affiliation: Department of Molecular Biology and Genetics, Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark.

papers.title: The energy sensor SnRK1 promotes starvation-induced autophagosome formation by modulating ATG13a phosphorylation in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Abstract In eukaryotes, autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved cellular degradation and recycling process that is tightly associated with cellular nutrient status. The energy sensor SNF1-RELATED KINASE 1 (SnRK1) is thought to sense nutrient starvation and induce autophagy, but how it regulates autophagosome formation in plant cells remains largely unknown. Here, we show that the SnRK1 α-catalytic subunit KIN10 regulates autophagosome formation in Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) by interacting with and phosphorylating AUTOPHAGY-RELATED PROTEIN 13a (ATG13a), a key component of the ATG1a–ATG13a protein kinase complex involved in autophagy initiation. KIN10 directly phosphorylates ATG13a in vitro and in vivo, inhibiting its ubiquitination and increasing its abundance. Moreover, we identified ten serine residues in ATG13a that are important for KIN10-mediated phosphorylation. Transgenic plants accumulating a nonphosphorylatable ATG13a variant with mutations of these ten residues were less tolerant of starvation than ATG13a-overexpressing plants and displayed accelerated leaf senescence and lower autophagic flux. The KIN10-mediated phosphorylation of ATG13a did not affect ATG1a–ATG13a complex formation; instead, it facilitated ATG1a phosphorylation, thereby promoting autophagosome formation. Therefore, our findings suggest that the KIN10–ATG13a module modulates SnRK1-mediated autophagosome formation, likely representing a key step in integrating energy sensing and autophagy initiation in plant cells.

papers.title: Spatial targeting and expansion prevention offer effective pathways to protect African maize from parasitic weeds
A pair of chitosan receptors confer broad-spectrum fungal resistance
papers.abstract: Chitosan, a major fungal cell wall component, activates plant immunity, yet the underlying perception mechanism remains unknown. In this study, we identified OsFID1, an apoplast-localized DUF26 domain protein, as a chitosan-binding receptor essential for chitosan-triggered immunity. OsFID1 forms a receptor complex with OsFID2, a plasma membrane–localized DUF26 receptor-like kinase, to mediate chitosan sensing and immune activation, requiring OsFID2 phosphorylation for function. The OsFID1-OsFID2 complex confers broad-spectrum resistance to fungal pathogens. OsFID1 homologs are conserved in land plants, which show chitosan-binding activity in both monocots and dicots. Ectopic expression of OsFID1 in wheat and maize enhanced fungal resistance without growth penalty. These findings uncover a conserved receptor complex for direct chitosan sensing, advancing our understanding of plant-fungus interactions and providing a potential strategy for engineering durable fungal resistance crops.

papers.title: Author Correction: Versatile molecular tools enabling customizable DNA methylation editing in Arabidopsis
Shading enhances Se accumulation in tea leaves through promoting CsMYB7-like-mediated conversion of Se (VI) to Se (IV)
papers.abstract: Limited selenium (Se) accumulation in agricultural products contributes to widespread dietary Se deficiency, posing a global nutritional threat. Efficient agronomic strategies to enhance Se biofortification in crops are still lacking. Here, we reveal the synergistic effects of shading and Se nanoparticles application on Se biofortification in tea leaves. Field experiments demonstrate that shading enhances Se accumulation in tea leaves under sufficient Se supply, through activating Se metabolism pathway. We identify CsAPR1 functions at the early stage of Se assimilation, catalyzing the reduction of Se (VI). The transcription of CsAPR1 is activated by CsMYB7-like and is further promoted by shading through interaction with CsbHLH70. Under sunlight, CsHY5 competes with CsbHLH70 for binding to CsMYB7-like, thereby attenuating CsMYB7-like-mediated transcription of CsAPR1 and suppressing Se accumulation in tea plants. Our findings reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying shade-induced enhancement of Se biofortification, offering insights and strategies for Se-enriched crop production.
papers.affiliation: Zhejiang Key Laboratory of Horticultural Crop Quality Improvement, Tea Research Institute, Zhejiang University

papers.title: RuBP availability contributes to the regulation of RUBISCO activity in Synechocystis
papers.abstract: Abstract RIBULOSE-1,5-BISPHOSPHATE CARBOXYLASE/OXYGENASE (RUBISCO) and the Calvin-Benson-Bassham (CBB) cycle assimilate most of the inorganic carbon on earth. Conserved CP12 proteins control diurnal C-assimilation of the CBB cycle. Their function originated in cyanobacteria that deactivate GLYCERALDEHYDE 3-PHOSPHATE DEHYDROGENASE (GAPDH) and PHOSPHORIBULOKINASE (PRK) during darkness by redox-regulated complex-formation with CP12. This mechanism indicates metabolic regulation of C-assimilation. We measured C-assimilation in vivo at the day/night transition by dynamic 13CO2 labeling and 1-C-positional monitoring of 13C-incorporation into 3-phosphoglycerate (3PGA) and aspartate of Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 grown with high (5%) CO2 supply. Unlike wild type, a Δcp12 mutant accumulated ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) and assimilated 13CO2 in darkness. We validated these observations by proteome measurements and orthogonal quantifications of RUBISCO abundances and specific activities. Complementation of Δcp12 with native CP12 and point-mutants of its GAPDH- and PRK-binding domains demonstrated that defective complex formation is causal for aberrant C-assimilation during darkness and that RuBP accumulation correlates significantly with the time-shifted 13C-incorporation into 3PGA. RUBISCO carboxylase activity is present throughout the diurnal cycle and depends on CP12-controlled substrate availability. 13C-positional analyses suggest dysregulated RuBP regeneration in Δcp12 during darkness via futile metabolic cycling through gluconeogenesis and the oxidative pentose phosphate path. We propose that blocked regeneration and rapid depletion of RuBP contributes to the regulation of RUBISCO activity at day-night transitions.
papers.affiliation: Max-Planck-Institute of Molecular Plant Physiology , Am Mühlenberg 1, 14476 Potsdam-Golm ,

papers.title: LMBD2 interacts with components of the ECH/YIP complex and contributes to post-Golgi trafficking in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Abstract The plant cell wall, composed primarily of polysaccharides, is essential for normal plant growth and development. Many of these polysaccharides are synthesized within and subsequently secreted via the endomembrane system. Mutations in genes including MURUS3 (MUR3), YPT/RAB GTPase-interacting protein 4 homologs (YIP4a/YIP4b), and ECHIDNA (ECH) result in dwarf plants, which is believed to be a consequence of impaired cell wall polysaccharide secretion. Here, we identify a LMBR1 (Limb Development Membrane Protein 1)-like membrane protein (LMBD2) and find that loss of LMBD2 suppresses the secretion and growth defects in the mur3, yip4a/yip4b, and ech mutants. LMBD2 localizes to the trans-Golgi apparatus and trans-Golgi network (TGN)/early endosome (EE), where it interacts with YIP4b and orchestrates TGN/EE-mediated trafficking. Furthermore, LMBD2 can competitively attenuate the interaction of YIP4b and ECH. Our findings establish LMBD2 as a component of endomembrane trafficking homeostasis in plant cells and offer new insights into endomembrane dynamics and their influence on plant development.
papers.affiliation: College of Agronomy, Qingdao Agricultural University , Qingdao 266109 ,

papers.title: Conserved DEAD-box RNA helicases regulate RNA silencing and plant immunity and are targeted by a powdery mildew effector
papers.abstract: Abstract RNA silencing is a conserved defense mechanism that protects plants against viruses, bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes. Although diverse pathogens have evolved effectors that suppress host RNA silencing, whether powdery mildew fungi exploit this strategy and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we identify CSEP0004, a secreted effector from the barley powdery mildew fungus Blumeria hordei, as an RNA silencing suppressor that promotes fungal virulence. CSEP0004 physically interacts with the evolutionarily conserved DEAD-box RNA helicases Hordeum vulgare RNA helicase 37 (HvRH37) and HvRH52. Genetic analyses demonstrate that HvRH37 and HvRH52 positively regulate chitin-triggered reactive oxygen species production, resistance to B. hordei, and small RNA accumulation in barley, while their Arabidopsis homologs AtRH11/37/52 perform conserved functions in small RNA accumulation. Mechanistically, HvRH37 and HvRH52 associate with HvAGO1, a core component of the RNA-induced silencing complex, and function as biochemically active RNA helicases capable of binding and unwinding double-stranded RNA. CSEP0004 disrupts the HvRH37/52–AGO1 association and inhibits HvRH37/52 helicase activity in a dose-dependent manner. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism by which a fungal effector suppresses host RNA silencing through targeting conserved DDX3-like DEAD-box RNA helicases, establishing these helicases as key regulators of RNAi-mediated immunity and identifying RNA helicase-dependent RNA remodeling as a critical regulatory node exploited by fungal pathogens.
papers.affiliation: Laboratory of Advanced Breeding Technologies, Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology, Chinese Academy of Sciences , Beijing 100101 ,
